decks.title: Rural Development — Part 1: Rural Credit and Agricultural Marketing
goals: Explain what rural development means and which areas need attention
Explain why rural households need credit and compare its institutional and non-institutional sources
Evaluate self-help groups and the problems of rural banking
Explain the problems of agricultural marketing and the measures taken to improve it

slides.heading: Rural Development
slides.body_md: Part 1 — **rural credit** and **agricultural marketing**: how farmers borrow and how they sell.

visual.alt: Route map of Part 1: what rural development means, why farmers borrow, who lends, self-help groups, selling the crop and better marketing
visual.caption: Part 1 at a glance

slides.narration: Most Indians still live in villages, and a large share of them depend on farming. Yet a farm family can work hard all season and still end up in debt. Why? Often because it borrowed at high interest or sold its crop at a poor price. In this part we study rural credit and agricultural marketing, two areas that decide how much of the harvest stays with the farmer.

slides.heading: What is rural development?
slides.body_md: Rural development is action to develop the **areas and people that lag behind** in the village economy.

rows: Secure land gives a reason to invest
Fair loans and fair prices raise farm income
New crops, methods and non-farm jobs

visual.alt: Table of areas needing attention for rural development: human capital, land reforms, credit and marketing, and productive activities and research, with why each matters

slides.narration: Rural development is not only about more crops. It means improving the lives of rural people by working on the areas that lag behind. These include literacy and health, land reforms, fair credit, better marketing, and new productive work. In this chapter the syllabus asks us to focus on credit, marketing, diversification and organic farming.

slides.heading: Why do farmers need credit?
slides.body_md: Farming has a **long gestation period**: spending comes months before income.

nodes.label: Sowing: pay for seeds, fertiliser, labour
Months of growth: family still needs money

visual.alt: Flow of the farm season: money is spent at sowing and during months of growth, income comes only at harvest and sale, and then the loan is repaid
visual.caption: Why farmers borrow: the gap between spending and earning

slides.narration: A farmer pays for seeds, fertiliser and labour at sowing, but is paid only after the harvest is sold, months later. In between, the family still needs food, medicine and money for weddings or emergencies. A farmer may also need a large sum for a pump or a pair of bullocks. So credit is a normal and necessary part of farm life.

slides.heading: Who lends in rural India?
slides.body_md: Two families of lenders: **non-institutional** and **institutional**.

nodes.label: Institutional: commercial banks, RRBs, cooperatives, SHGs
NABARD: apex body that coordinates and refinances

visual.alt: Tree of rural credit sources: non-institutional sources are moneylenders, traders and landlords; institutional sources are commercial banks, Regional Rural Banks, cooperatives and self-help groups, coordinated by NABARD
visual.caption: Two families of lenders

slides.narration: Rural credit comes from two kinds of sources. Non-institutional lenders are private: moneylenders, traders and landlords. They lend quickly but often at very high interest, and a trader who lends may also force the farmer to sell him the crop cheaply. Institutional sources are regulated: commercial banks, Regional Rural Banks, cooperatives and self-help groups, with NABARD at the top coordinating them.

slides.heading: Quick check: sources of credit
slides.body_md: Which one is a **non-institutional** source of credit?
slides.narration: Ask: is this lender regulated by law and part of the banking system, or is it a private person lending on his own terms?

slides.heading: The growth of rural banking
slides.body_md: A **multi-agency approach**: many institutions, one goal of cheaper credit for villages.

rows: Major commercial banks nationalised; rural branches expand
NABARD set up as the apex body for rural financing
Self-help groups linked to banks spread microcredit

visual.alt: Timeline table of rural banking: 1969 nationalisation of major banks, 1975 Regional Rural Banks, 1982 NABARD, and from the 1990s self-help groups linked to banks
visual.caption: Multi-agency approach: many kinds of institutions, one goal.

slides.narration: After major commercial banks were nationalised in nineteen sixty nine, they were asked to open branches in villages and lend to agriculture. Regional Rural Banks followed in nineteen seventy five, and NABARD was set up in nineteen eighty two as the apex body to coordinate and refinance rural lenders. Cooperative credit societies and, later, self-help groups completed the system.

slides.heading: Quick check: the apex body
slides.body_md: Which body coordinates the institutions that finance rural areas?
slides.narration: Think of the body set up in nineteen eighty two whose name contains both agriculture and rural development.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: what a moneylender really costs
slides.body_md: An imagined farmer borrows ₹30,000 for 4 months. Compare a moneylender at **4 per cent a month** with a bank at **8 per cent a year**.
bullets: Step 1 — Check the unit of each rate: per month or per year.
Step 2 — Simple interest = principal × rate ÷ 100 × time (in the same unit as the rate).
Step 3 — Moneylender: ₹4,800; bank: ₹800.
Step 4 — Conclude: the bank saves her ₹4,000.

visual.alt: Table working out interest on an imagined loan of 30,000 rupees for 4 months: 4,800 rupees from the moneylender, 800 rupees from the bank, a difference of 4,000 rupees
visual.caption: Watch the unit of the rate: a month or a year.

slides.narration: Let us compare. The moneylender charges four per cent a month, so for four months that is sixteen per cent of thirty thousand rupees, which is four thousand eight hundred rupees. The bank charges eight per cent a year; four months is one third of a year, so the interest is just eight hundred rupees. The same loan costs six times as much from the moneylender.

This is why the spread of institutional credit matters so much: every rupee saved on interest stays with the farm family. It also explains how a family that borrows repeatedly from moneylenders can fall into a debt trap.

slides.heading: Self-help groups and microcredit
slides.body_md: Small groups, mostly of women, who **save together** and **borrow together**.

nodes.label: Save a small sum every month
Lend to members at fair interest
Bank loan to the group without collateral

visual.alt: Flow of how a self-help group works: members save regularly, lend to each other at fair interest, build a repayment record and then get a bank loan as a group without collateral
visual.caption: How an SHG works

slides.narration: A self-help group is a small group, often of ten to twenty women, who save a small amount every month. The pooled fund is lent to members at fair interest. Once the group has a good repayment record, a bank can lend to it without asking for land or gold, because the group guarantees repayment. This is called microcredit.

slides.heading: SHGs: strengths and limits
columns:
**Strengths**
- Habit of thrift
- Loans without collateral
- Women gain income and confidence
- Less dependence on moneylenders

**Limits**
- Loans are small
- Often used for consumption
- Need skills and markets to raise incomes
- Some groups break up

visual.alt: Flow from thrift to credit to enterprise to income, the path an SHG hopes to follow
visual.caption: The hoped-for path

slides.narration: Self-help groups have brought credit to many women who had none. But a fair judgement must include the limits. The loans are small, and many are used for household needs rather than for starting an enterprise. To raise incomes for good, groups need training, skills and access to markets as well as credit.

slides.heading: Problems of institutional credit

rows: Small and marginal farmers poorly reached
Banks lose the ability to lend again
Credit goes where risk seems low

visual.alt: Table of problems of institutional rural credit and their effects: small farmers poorly reached, defaults, preference for larger borrowers, weak link with rural savings

slides.narration: Rural banking has grown a great deal, but it has weaknesses. Many small and marginal farmers and landless workers are still not reached, so they borrow from moneylenders. Loan defaults weaken banks. Lenders have often preferred larger borrowers who seem safer. And banks have done less to collect rural savings that could be lent locally.

slides.heading: Selling the crop: agricultural marketing
slides.body_md: Marketing = everything that happens to the produce **between the field and the buyer**.

visual.alt: Flow of the stages of agricultural marketing: assemble, grade and pack, store, transport and sell
visual.caption: Marketing is everything between the field and the buyer

slides.narration: Growing a good crop is half the battle. The other half is selling it well. Agricultural marketing includes assembling the produce, grading and packing it, storing it, transporting it and finally selling it. At each step, the farmer can gain or lose.

slides.heading: Where farmers lose money

rows: Paid for less than he sold

visual.alt: Table of problems farmers face when selling: faulty weights, no price information, no storage, and loans tied to the crop, with how each causes a loss

slides.narration: Without regulation, farmers often lose at the market. Traders may use faulty weights and manipulate accounts. Farmers may not know the prices in other markets. Without storage, they must sell at harvest when prices are lowest; this is called a distress sale. And a farmer who borrowed from a trader may be forced to sell to him at a low price.

slides.heading: Quick check: distress sale
slides.body_md: An onion grower sells his whole crop on harvest day because he has nowhere to keep it. What is this?
slides.narration: Look for the reason he had no choice about when to sell.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: the price spread
slides.body_md: Consumers in an imagined city pay ₹35 a kg for onions; the farmer gets ₹14.
bullets: Step 1 — Price spread = 35 − 14 = ₹21 a kg.
Step 2 — Farmer's share = 14 ÷ 35 × 100 = 40 per cent.
Step 3 — Split the spread: transport ₹4, wholesaler ₹7, retailer ₹10.
Step 4 — Interpret: fewer middlemen would leave more for both farmer and consumer.

slides.narration: The price spread is the gap between what the consumer pays and what the farmer receives. Here it is twenty one rupees a kilo, and the farmer keeps only forty per cent of the final price. Part of the spread pays for real services like transport, but layers of middlemen take the rest. Marketing reforms try to shrink this gap.

slides.heading: Measures to improve marketing

rows: Open auctions, correct weights, prompt payment
Farmers sell together and share the margin
Floor price for farmers; grain for consumers in shortages
Farmers' markets, contracts with processors and retailers

visual.alt: Table of measures to improve agricultural marketing: regulated markets, infrastructure, cooperative marketing, MSP with buffer stocks and the public distribution system, and direct channels

slides.narration: The government has tried several measures. Regulated markets bring open auctions and correct weights. Roads, warehouses and cold storages cut wastage and distress sales. Cooperatives let farmers sell together. Minimum support prices, buffer stocks and the public distribution system protect farmers and consumers. And direct channels, such as farmers' markets, let growers sell straight to buyers.

slides.heading: MSP, buffer stocks and ration shops

visual.alt: Flow from the minimum support price announced before sowing, to government purchase, buffer stocks in warehouses, and release through ration shops
visual.caption: One chain protects farmers and consumers

slides.narration: Here is how one chain works. The government announces a minimum support price for certain crops before sowing. Its agencies buy grain at that price, so farmers have a floor. The grain is kept as buffer stock in warehouses. When harvests fail or prices rise, it is released through ration shops, protecting consumers.

slides.heading: Summary of Part 1

rows: Action on the lagging areas and people of the village economy
Long gap between spending and harvest; family needs
Banks after 1969, RRBs 1975, cooperatives, NABARD 1982, SHGs
Malpractices, no information, no storage, tied sales
Regulated markets, infrastructure, cooperatives, MSP, buffer stocks, PDS, direct channels

visual.alt: Summary table of Part 1: rural development, the need for credit, credit institutions, marketing problems and measures

slides.narration: To sum up Part 1. Rural development means working on the lagging areas of the village economy. Farmers need credit because of the long gap between spending and earning. Banks, Regional Rural Banks, cooperatives, NABARD and self-help groups have widened cheaper credit, though the poorest are not fully reached. Marketing reforms aim to give farmers a fair share of the final price.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: Credit: always link **need** to the **gestation period** and family needs.
Dates: **1969** nationalisation, **1975** RRBs, **1982** NABARD.
SHGs: mention **collateral-free** bank linkage and **women**; evaluate with limits.
Marketing: name the malpractice, then the matching measure.
Numericals: check whether the interest rate is **per month** or **per year**.

visual.alt: Flow of a strong answer: problem, cause, measure and effect
visual.caption: Structure for 3 and 5 mark answers

slides.narration: A few tips. When asked why farmers need credit, mention the long gestation period and family needs. Learn the three dates: nineteen sixty nine, seventy five and eighty two. For self-help groups, stress loans without collateral and the role of women, and give limits if asked to evaluate. In marketing answers, match each problem with a measure. In numericals, check the unit of the interest rate.

decks.title: Rural Development — Part 2: Cooperatives, Diversification and Organic Farming
goals: Explain how dairy cooperatives on the Anand pattern help rural households
Explain the two aspects of agricultural diversification and why it is needed
Describe allied activities, non-farm work and the role of information technology
Evaluate organic farming, with its benefits and limitations

slides.heading: Rural Development — Part 2
slides.body_md: **Cooperatives**, **diversification** and **organic farming**: new ways to earn and to farm.

visual.alt: Route map of Part 2: dairy cooperatives, diversification, allied activities, non-farm work and IT, and organic farming
visual.caption: Part 2 at a glance

slides.narration: In Part 1 we saw how farmers borrow and sell. Now we look at three ideas that change how rural families earn and farm. Cooperatives let small producers act together. Diversification spreads work and risk beyond a single crop. And organic farming offers a more sustainable way of growing food. Each has strengths and limits we must be ready to weigh.

slides.heading: Dairy cooperatives: the Anand pattern
slides.body_md: Village societies, district unions and state federations, owned by **milk producers**.

nodes.label: Member pours milk at village society
Tested and paid by quantity and fat
State federation sells the brand in cities

visual.alt: Flow of a dairy cooperative on the Anand pattern: members pour milk at the village society, are paid by quantity and fat, the district union processes it and the state federation sells it in cities
visual.caption: The three-tier cooperative pattern

slides.narration: The best-known example of cooperative marketing is dairying. Beginning in Anand in Gujarat, milk producers formed village societies. Each member pours milk, which is tested and paid for by quantity and fat. District unions process it, and a state federation sells it under one brand in cities. From nineteen seventy, Operation Flood spread this pattern to many states, helping India become one of the largest milk producers in the world.

slides.heading: Quick check: where it began
slides.body_md: Where did the cooperative dairy model behind Operation Flood begin?
slides.narration: Recall the town in Gujarat whose milk cooperative became a model for the whole country.

slides.heading: Why cooperatives help

rows: Paid often, by quantity and quality
The cooperative itself processes and sells
Women do much of the dairy work

visual.alt: Table of gains from dairy cooperatives: regular income, no middlemen, services such as vet care and feed, and income for women

slides.narration: Why do members gain? They are paid regularly and fairly. Because the cooperative processes and sells the milk itself, there are no middlemen taking a margin. Members also get services such as veterinary care and cattle feed. And since women do much of the dairy work, cooperatives give many rural women an income of their own.

slides.heading: What is diversification?

nodes.label: Change in cropping pattern: more fruits, vegetables, oilseeds, flowers
Shift of workers to allied and non-farm activities

visual.alt: Diagram of the two aspects of diversification: a change in cropping pattern, and a shift of workers to allied and non-farm activities
visual.caption: Two aspects

slides.narration: Diversification has two aspects. The first is a change in the cropping pattern, from mainly food grains to a wider range including fruits, vegetables, oilseeds and flowers. The second is a shift of workers from crop farming to allied activities such as livestock and fisheries, and to non-farm work such as processing, crafts and services.

slides.heading: Why diversify?
slides.body_md: Crop farming alone is **seasonal** and, where it depends on rain, **risky**.
bullets: Work for only part of the year
One bad monsoon can wipe out income
A growing rural workforce needs more productive jobs
slides.narration: Why is diversification needed? In much of India, crop farming gives work for only part of the year, and in rain-fed areas one poor monsoon can destroy a family's income. The rural workforce is also growing, and farms cannot absorb everyone productively. Other activities provide work in the off-season and spread the risk.

slides.heading: Allied and non-farm activities

rows: Inland ponds and rivers; sea fishing

visual.alt: Table of allied and non-farm activities: animal husbandry, fisheries, horticulture and non-farm work, with examples and why each helps

slides.narration: Here are the main options. Animal husbandry, with cattle, goats and poultry, gives a steady income and needs little land. Fisheries, inland and marine, employ men and women. Horticulture, growing fruits, vegetables, flowers and spices, earns more per acre. And non-farm work, like agro-processing, crafts and tourism, creates jobs outside the crop season.

slides.heading: Quick check: mixed farming
slides.body_md: A family keeps goats and cows along with its millet crop. What is the main advantage?
slides.narration: Think about what happens to the family's income in a year when the rains fail.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: how much comes from outside crops?
slides.body_md: An imagined household earns ₹54,000 from crops, ₹18,000 from goats and ₹18,000 from a fish pond in a year.
bullets: Step 1 — Total income = ₹90,000.
Step 3 — Share = 36,000 ÷ 90,000 × 100 = 40 per cent.
Step 4 — Interpret: if the crop fails, much of the income survives.

slides.narration: Let us measure diversification for one imagined family. Its total income is ninety thousand rupees, of which thirty six thousand comes from goats and fish. That is forty per cent of its income from outside crops. In a drought year the crop income may collapse, but the goats and the fish pond keep a large part of the family's earnings safe.

slides.heading: Horticulture and fisheries up close
slides.body_md: High-value crops and fish bring **income per acre** and **work for women**.

sections.heading: 1. Meaning of rural development
sections.body_md:
Rural development is action aimed at the **areas and sections that lag behind** in the village economy. Areas needing attention include **human capital** (literacy, especially female literacy, skills and health), **land reforms**, **credit** and **marketing**, **productive activities** including non-farm work, and **research** into better methods.

This chapter studies credit, marketing, diversification and organic farming. (Poverty and Infrastructure are not in the 2026-27 syllabus.)

sections.heading: 2. Rural credit: need and sources
sections.body_md:
**Need:** farming has a **long gestation period** between spending on inputs and getting income; there are fixed investments (pumps, cattle, wells) and family needs (illness, weddings, ceremonies).

**Non-institutional sources:** moneylenders, traders and landlords. Quick and informal, but usually at **very high interest**; loans may be tied to selling the crop to the lender, which can create a **debt trap**.

**Institutional sources:** commercial banks (rural branches grew after **nationalisation in 1969**), **Regional Rural Banks** (**1975**), cooperative credit societies and banks, land development banks, and **self-help groups**. **NABARD** (**1982**) is the apex body that coordinates and refinances rural lenders.

sections.heading: 3. Self-help groups and problems of rural banking
sections.body_md:
**SHGs:** small groups, mostly of women, that build a common fund from regular small savings, lend to members at reasonable interest, and after a good repayment record borrow from banks **without collateral**. This is **microcredit**. SHGs encourage thrift and give women income and a voice; their loans are small and often used for consumption, so they need skills and market links too.

**Problems of institutional credit:** it does not reach enough small and marginal farmers and landless workers; **loan defaults** weaken banks; lenders have preferred larger borrowers; and mobilising rural savings has been slow. Moneylenders therefore survive.

sections.heading: 4. Agricultural marketing
sections.body_md:
**Meaning:** assembling, storing, processing, grading, packing, transporting and selling farm produce.

**Problems:** faulty weights and manipulated accounts; no information on prices elsewhere; no storage, which forces **distress sales**; loans tied to selling to the lender.

**Measures:**
1. **Regulated markets** for open, orderly and transparent trading.
2. **Physical infrastructure**: roads, railways, warehouses, cold storages, processing units.
3. **Cooperative marketing**, so producers sell together.
4. **Policy instruments**: **minimum support prices** for certain crops; **buffer stocks** of wheat and rice held by the Food Corporation of India; the **public distribution system**.
5. **Alternative channels**: farmers' markets where growers sell directly to consumers in several states, and contracts with processing firms and retail chains.

The **price spread** is the gap between the consumer's price and the farmer's price; reforms aim to narrow it.

sections.heading: 5. Cooperatives and dairying
sections.body_md: Cooperatives let small producers act together in credit, marketing and processing. The best-known example is **dairying**: the **Anand pattern** in Gujarat (village societies → district unions → state federation) was spread across states by **Operation Flood**, begun in **1970**. Members are paid by quantity and fat content; the cooperative processes and sells the milk, removing middlemen; members get services such as veterinary care and feed. Dairying gives regular income, much of it earned by **women**, and India has become one of the world's largest milk producers.

sections.heading: 6. Diversification into productive activities
sections.body_md:
**Two aspects:** (1) a **change in cropping pattern** towards a wider range of crops; (2) a **shift of workers** from crop farming to **allied activities** and **non-farm** work.

**Why:** crop farming is seasonal and, in rain-fed areas, risky; the rural workforce needs more productive, year-round work.

**Animal husbandry:** cattle, buffaloes, goats, poultry; regular income, suits small and landless families, reduces risk (mixed farming).
**Fisheries:** inland (ponds, rivers, reservoirs) and marine; women often process and sell the catch.
**Horticulture:** fruits, vegetables, flowers, spices, medicinal and aromatic plants; high value per acre, labour-intensive, links to processing and export.
**Non-farm work:** agro-processing, food processing, crafts, pottery, tourism.
**Information technology:** weather and crop advice, market prices, online records and services, and new rural jobs; limited by weak connectivity and digital skills.

sections.heading: 7. Organic farming
sections.body_md:
**Meaning:** a whole system of farming that restores, maintains and enhances ecological balance, using **compost, manure, green manure and natural pest control** instead of synthetic fertilisers and pesticides.

**Benefits:** sustainable for soil and water; **cheaper on-farm inputs**; food free of chemical residues; demand at home and abroad; **more labour per acre**, so more rural jobs.

**Limitations:** **lower yields in the early years**; **shorter shelf life**; less choice of off-season produce; farmers need awareness, **certification** and marketing support. A balanced view: valuable for many crops and regions, with support during the transition. (One frequently cited example: Sikkim was declared a fully organic state in 2016.)

questions.stem_md: Rural development mainly means

options.text_md: moving most rural people to cities so that villages become smaller
action to develop the areas that lag behind in the village economy and improve the lives of rural people
raising the output of large factories located in villages
replacing farming completely with services in every village

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** action to develop the areas that lag behind in the village economy and improve the lives of rural people. Rural development focuses on the lagging areas and people of the village economy: skills, health, land, credit, marketing and productive work. It does not aim to empty villages, build big factories there or abolish farming.

questions.stem_md: State any four areas that need attention for the development of rural India.
questions.solution_md: Any four distinct areas from human capital, land reforms, credit, marketing, productive activities and research.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Human capital**: literacy, especially of women, skills and health.
2. **Land reforms** and better use of local resources.
3. **Credit** at fair rates and **marketing** facilities.
4. **Productive non-farm work** and research into better farm methods.

questions.stem_md: Why do farmers need credit more than most other producers?

options.text_md: Farm output is sold before the seeds are sown
Farmers never have any family expenses
Banks require every farmer to borrow each season
There is a long gap between sowing and harvest, while seeds, fertiliser and family needs must be paid for in between

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** There is a long gap between sowing and harvest, while seeds, fertiliser and family needs must be paid for in between. Farming has a long gestation period: money is spent on inputs at sowing but income comes only after harvest, and household needs continue in between. The other options are untrue.

questions.stem_md: Which of the following is a **non-institutional** source of rural credit?

options.text_md: A village moneylender
A Regional Rural Bank
A primary agricultural credit society
A nationalised commercial bank

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** A village moneylender. Moneylenders, traders and landlords lend privately, outside any regulated institution. RRBs, cooperative credit societies and commercial banks are institutional sources.

questions.stem_md: Ramesh, a small farmer in an imagined village of Vidarbha, borrows from a trader who also buys his cotton. Which outcome is **most likely**?

options.text_md: He will get the highest market price because the trader is his lender
He pays no interest because the loan is informal
He must sell his cotton to the trader at a low price fixed by the lender, and the debt keeps growing
His loan will be refinanced by NABARD

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** He must sell his cotton to the trader at a low price fixed by the lender, and the debt keeps growing. Lenders who are also buyers tie the loan to the crop: the farmer sells at the lender's price, pays high interest and often remains in debt. Informal loans carry interest, and NABARD does not refinance private traders.

questions.stem_md: The expansion of commercial bank branches into rural areas got a major push after

options.text_md: the first census of 1881
the setting up of the Planning Commission in 1950
the nationalisation of major commercial banks in 1969
the start of GST in 2017

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** the nationalisation of major commercial banks in 1969. After major banks were nationalised in 1969, the government directed them to open rural branches and lend to priority sectors such as agriculture. The other events are unrelated to rural banking.

questions.stem_md: Regional Rural Banks were set up in India in
questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** 1975. RRBs were created in 1975 to give credit to small farmers, labourers, artisans and small entrepreneurs in rural areas.

questions.stem_md: Which body was set up in 1982 as the apex institution to coordinate the institutions financing rural areas?

options.text_md: Reserve Bank of India
Food Corporation of India
National Dairy Development Board
NABARD

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** NABARD. The National Bank for Agriculture and Rural Development (NABARD), set up in 1982, coordinates and refinances rural credit institutions. The RBI is the central bank; FCI handles food stocks; NDDB promotes dairying.

questions.stem_md: Which statement best describes a **self-help group** (SHG)?

options.text_md: A large company that lends to farmers at high interest
A small group of rural people, often women, who pool small savings and lend to members, and may then borrow from banks
A government office that buys grain at the minimum support price
A cooperative that sells milk in cities

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** A small group of rural people, often women, who pool small savings and lend to members, and may then borrow from banks. SHGs encourage thrift: members save small amounts regularly, lend to each other at reasonable rates and can get bank loans as a group. The other options describe lenders, FCI and a dairy cooperative.

questions.stem_md: Why can an SHG member get a loan without pledging land or gold?

options.text_md: The group itself guarantees repayment, and members know and check each other
Banks are not allowed to ask anyone for security
SHG loans never have to be repaid
The moneylender pledges his own land for her

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** The group itself guarantees repayment, and members know and check each other. Group responsibility and peer monitoring replace collateral: the group decides, guarantees and follows up on repayment. Loans are repaid, banks may take security from other borrowers, and the moneylender has no role.

questions.stem_md: Which is a widely discussed **weakness** of institutional rural credit?

options.text_md: It charges higher interest than moneylenders
Poor recovery of loans and a smaller share of credit reaching small and marginal farmers
It has completely replaced informal lenders in every village
It gives loans only to industrial firms in cities

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Poor recovery of loans and a smaller share of credit reaching small and marginal farmers. Institutional credit has expanded but faces defaults and does not reach enough small and marginal farmers, so informal lenders survive. Its rates are usually lower than moneylenders', and it does lend to farmers.

Informal lender; quick loans at high interest
Bank set up in 1975 for small rural borrowers

questions.solution_md: **Key:** (a)–(r), (b)–(p), (c)–(s), (d)–(q). Moneylenders are informal and costly; credit societies are cooperatives of members; RRBs are banks for small rural borrowers; SHGs pool thrift and lend within the group.

questions.stem_md: An imagined farmer needs ₹20,000 for 6 months. A moneylender charges 5 per cent **a month** (simple interest); a cooperative bank charges 7 per cent **a year** (simple interest). How much interest (in ₹) does she save by borrowing from the bank?
questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Moneylender's interest = 20,000 × 5/100 × 6 = ₹6,000.
Step 2: Bank's interest = 20,000 × 7/100 × 6/12 = ₹700.
Step 3: Saving = 6,000 − 700 = ₹5,300.

questions.stem_md: An imagined SHG has 15 members. Each saves ₹200 a month. What is the group's total saving after 12 months (in ₹)?
questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Saving = members × monthly saving × months.
Step 2: 15 × 200 × 12 = ₹36,000.

questions.stem_md: Distinguish between institutional and non-institutional sources of rural credit, with one example of each.
questions.solution_md: Contrast regulation and terms, with one example on each side.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Institutional** sources are regulated bodies that lend at **fair, stated rates**, e.g. a commercial bank, an RRB or a cooperative credit society.
2. **Non-institutional** sources are private lenders, often charging **high interest** with no regulation, e.g. moneylenders, traders and landlords.

questions.stem_md: How do self-help groups help reduce rural dependence on moneylenders? Give two points.
questions.solution_md: Internal thrift and lending, then bank linkage without security.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. Members **save regularly** and borrow from the group's own fund at **reasonable interest**, so small needs no longer go to the moneylender.
2. After a record of repayment, the group gets **bank loans without collateral**, opening formal credit to poor women who had none.

questions.stem_md: Give two reasons why moneylenders still lend to many farmers despite the growth of banks.
questions.solution_md: Access barriers at banks and the convenience or purposes covered by moneylenders.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. Small and **marginal farmers** without land titles or security find it **hard to get bank loans**, while moneylenders lend quickly without paperwork.
2. Banks may be **far away** and slow, and they do not lend for family needs such as weddings or illness, which moneylenders do.

questions.stem_md: Explain three reasons why rural households need credit.
questions.solution_md: One point each on working capital, fixed investment and household or emergency needs.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Long gestation**: farmers spend on seeds, fertiliser and labour at sowing but are paid only after harvest.
2. **Investment**: buying a pump, cattle, or digging a well needs a large sum at once.
3. **Family needs**: weddings, illness, deaths and ceremonies, and survival after a crop failure, often require borrowing.

questions.stem_md: Rural banking has grown since 1969, yet it faces problems. Explain any three.
questions.solution_md: Three distinct problems: reach, recovery and the bias or deposit side.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Insufficient reach**: credit still does not reach many small and marginal farmers and landless workers, who remain with moneylenders.
2. **Poor recovery**: defaults on farm loans weaken banks' ability to lend again.
3. **Weak focus**: banks have often preferred larger, safer borrowers, and **mobilising rural savings** has been slow.

questions.stem_md: Describe the institutional structure of rural credit in India and explain how it has tried to free farmers from moneylenders.
questions.solution_md: Four institutions or links in the system, then how they reduce dependence on moneylenders, with a balanced closing remark.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Commercial banks**: after nationalisation in **1969**, they opened rural branches and lent to agriculture as a priority sector.
2. **Regional Rural Banks** (from **1975**) serve small farmers, labourers and artisans.
3. **Cooperative credit societies and banks** lend to members; land development banks give longer loans.
4. **NABARD** (**1982**) coordinates and refinances these institutions.
5. **SHGs** pool savings and borrow from banks without collateral, reaching poor women. Together these give **cheaper, regulated credit**, so farmers depend less on moneylenders' high interest and tied sales, though coverage of the poorest is still incomplete.

questions.stem_md: Evaluate the role of self-help groups and microcredit in rural development.
questions.solution_md: Benefits (thrift, credit, linkage, empowerment) and limitations, ending in a judgement.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Thrift**: members save small amounts regularly, building a common fund.
2. **Fair credit**: they lend to members at reasonable rates for small needs, replacing costly informal loans.
3. **Bank linkage**: a repayment record lets groups borrow from banks **without collateral**.
4. **Empowerment**: most members are **women**, who gain income, confidence and a voice in decisions.
5. **Limits**: loans are small and often used for **consumption** rather than production, and some groups collapse without training or markets. On balance SHGs widen access to credit, but they need links to **skills and markets** to raise incomes lastingly.

questions.stem_md: Agricultural marketing covers

options.text_md: only the sowing and harvesting of crops
only the advertising of fertilisers on television
assembling, storing, processing, grading, packing, transporting and selling farm produce
only the export of food grains

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** assembling, storing, processing, grading, packing, transporting and selling farm produce. Marketing is the whole chain of activities from collecting produce to its sale, including storage, processing, grading, packing and transport. Sowing and harvesting are production; advertising and export are narrow parts at most.

questions.stem_md: A vegetable grower in an imagined village near Nashik sells his whole onion crop on the day of harvest at a very low price because he has nowhere to keep it. This is an example of

options.text_md: regulated marketing
buffer stocking
organic farming
distress sale due to lack of storage

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** distress sale due to lack of storage. Without storage he is forced to sell immediately, whatever the price: a distress sale. Regulated markets, buffer stocks and organic farming are unrelated to his problem.

questions.stem_md: The main purpose of **regulating** agricultural markets is to

options.text_md: fix the same price for every crop in every season
stop farmers from selling to private traders
collect a new tax from consumers
create orderly and transparent conditions so that farmers get fair prices

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** create orderly and transparent conditions so that farmers get fair prices. Regulated markets check malpractices such as faulty weights and hidden commissions, making trading transparent so that farmers get fair prices. They do not fix all prices, ban private traders or exist to tax consumers.

questions.stem_md: The **minimum support price** (MSP) helps farmers mainly by

options.text_md: guaranteeing that all crops will be sold abroad
giving free seeds to every farmer
assuring a price at which the government will buy certain crops, which protects them from very low prices
fixing the retail price that consumers pay in shops

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** assuring a price at which the government will buy certain crops, which protects them from very low prices. MSP is the price announced before sowing at which government agencies buy notified crops, so farmers are protected if market prices fall. It is not an export guarantee, a seed scheme or a retail price.

questions.stem_md: A year of poor rains raises grain prices in an imagined state. Which marketing measure helps the government keep prices in check?

options.text_md: Closing all regulated markets
Releasing grain from buffer stocks through the public distribution system
Banning cold storages
Withdrawing the minimum support price

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Releasing grain from buffer stocks through the public distribution system. Grain bought earlier and held as buffer stock can be released through ration shops when supply falls, which keeps prices in check. The other steps would worsen supply or marketing.

questions.stem_md: Farmers' markets where growers sell straight to consumers mainly benefit **both** sides because

options.text_md: fewer middlemen take a margin, so farmers get more and consumers pay less
the government pays every buyer a subsidy
prices there are always fixed at MSP
only exported crops are sold there

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** fewer middlemen take a margin, so farmers get more and consumers pay less. Cutting out intermediaries narrows the price spread, so part of the margin goes to the farmer and part to the consumer. Such markets do not pay buyers subsidies, are not tied to MSP and sell local produce.

questions.stem_md: Which is the most likely result of building cold storages near potato-growing villages?

options.text_md: Potato output will fall to zero
Farmers can wait for better prices instead of selling everything at harvest
Farmers will have to pay higher interest to moneylenders
Consumers will be unable to buy potatoes out of season

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Farmers can wait for better prices instead of selling everything at harvest. Storage lets farmers spread sales over the year and avoid harvest-time gluts, and it also supplies potatoes out of season. It does not cut output or raise interest.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Without regulation, farmers often receive less than the fair value of their produce.

**Reason (R):** Traders may use faulty weights, manipulate accounts and keep farmers unaware of market prices.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Both are true, and R explains A: such malpractices and lack of price information take away part of what farmers should earn.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Minimum support prices reduce the risk of a crash in farmers' income for the crops covered.

**Reason (R):** Under MSP, the government buys every crop grown in India at a fixed price.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** A is true: an assured purchase price protects farmers of covered crops. R is false: MSP covers only certain notified crops, and procurement is limited to them.

questions.stem_md: True or false? Buffer stocks of food grains are held so that grain can be supplied to consumers when production falls or prices rise.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: **True.** Grains procured in good years are stored and released through the public distribution system in shortages, protecting consumers.

questions.stem_md: The difference between the price paid by the consumer and the price received by the farmer is called the price ___.
questions.solution_md: It is the price spread; it goes to transporters, traders and other intermediaries.

questions.stem_md: Arrange these stages in the marketing of a wheat crop in a sensible order.

options.text_md: Transporting it to buyers and selling it
Harvesting and assembling the grain
Storing it in a warehouse
Grading and packing it in bags

questions.solution_md: **Correct order:** (b) → (d) → (c) → (a). Grain is first assembled, then graded and packed, stored until sale, and finally moved to buyers and sold.

marking_scheme.step: Complete correct sequence (all items in place)

questions.stem_md: In an imagined town, consumers pay ₹40 a kg for tomatoes, but the grower receives only ₹12 a kg. What percentage of the consumer's price reaches the grower?
questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Farmer's share = farmer's price ÷ consumer's price × 100.
Step 2: 12 ÷ 40 × 100 = 30 per cent.

questions.stem_md: An imagined farmer has 50 quintals of wheat. At harvest the price is ₹1,800 a quintal; three months later it is ₹2,200. Storing in a warehouse costs ₹100 a quintal for that period. How much more (in ₹) does she earn by storing and selling later?
questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Extra price per quintal = 2,200 − 1,800 = ₹400.
Step 2: Net gain per quintal = 400 − 100 = ₹300.
Step 3: Total = 50 × 300 = ₹15,000.

questions.stem_md: A trader's faulty scale shows 95 kg when 100 kg of chillies is weighed. At ₹30 a kg, how much (in ₹) does the farmer lose on this one sale?
questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Weight lost = 100 − 95 = 5 kg.
Step 2: Loss = 5 × 30 = ₹150.

questions.stem_md: State any two problems faced by farmers in selling their produce.
questions.solution_md: Any two genuine marketing problems, each briefly explained.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Malpractices** by traders: faulty weights and manipulated accounts reduce what the farmer is paid.
2. **No storage and little price information**: farmers sell at harvest at low prices, often to the trader who lent them money.

questions.stem_md: How can better roads and cold storage improve a vegetable grower's income?
questions.solution_md: Link each facility to a better price or wider market.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Roads** let her reach **larger markets** quickly and cheaply, so she is not tied to one local buyer.
2. **Cold storage** keeps vegetables fresh, so she can **sell when prices are better** instead of making a distress sale.

questions.stem_md: Explain any three measures taken to improve agricultural marketing in India.
questions.solution_md: Three measures, each with how it helps the farmer.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Regulated markets**: orderly, transparent auctions and correct weights so farmers get fair prices.
2. **Physical infrastructure**: roads, warehouses, cold storages and processing units that reduce wastage and distress sales.
3. **Policy support**: **minimum support prices**, **buffer stocks** and the **public distribution system** protect both farmers and consumers.

questions.stem_md: What are alternative marketing channels? Explain how they help farmers, with two examples of such channels.
questions.solution_md: Meaning, two kinds of channel, and the benefit to farmers.

answer.model_answer_md: Alternative channels let farmers **sell directly** to consumers or large buyers, bypassing layers of middlemen. Examples: **farmers' markets** run in several states where growers sell straight to city households, and **contracts with food-processing firms or retail chains** that agree a price in advance. They **narrow the price spread**, raise farmers' share and reduce price uncertainty.

questions.stem_md: Why do Indian farmers often fail to get a fair price for their produce? Explain the measures taken by the government to improve agricultural marketing.
questions.solution_md: Two problems, then three measures with their effect.

answer.model_answer_md:
**Problems:**
1. **Malpractices**: faulty weights, hidden deductions and manipulated accounts.
2. **No storage or price information**, so farmers sell at harvest or to the lender who financed them.

**Measures:**
3. **Regulated markets** that make trading transparent.
4. **Infrastructure**: roads, warehouses, cold storages and processing that cut wastage.
5. **Cooperative marketing** and policy tools: **MSP**, **buffer stocks** held by the Food Corporation of India and the **public distribution system**, plus direct farmers' markets. These raise the farmer's share, though private trade still dominates in many areas.

questions.stem_md: The cooperative model of dairying that inspired Operation Flood began in

options.text_md: Ludhiana, Punjab
Kochi, Kerala
Guwahati, Assam
Anand, Gujarat

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Anand, Gujarat. The Anand pattern of milk cooperatives in Gujarat became the model that Operation Flood spread to other states.

questions.stem_md: Under **Operation Flood**, milk producers

options.text_md: pool their milk in village cooperatives, which process and market it and pay them fair prices
sell all their milk to foreign companies
are paid by the government whether or not they supply milk
must give up crop farming completely

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** pool their milk in village cooperatives, which process and market it and pay them fair prices. Farmers form village cooperatives; milk is collected, graded, processed and sold in cities through a cooperative network, and producers are paid by quantity and quality. The other options misdescribe the programme.

questions.stem_md: True or false? A dairy cooperative that collects, processes and sells its members' milk reduces the role of middlemen.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: **True.** The cooperative itself does the work that private traders did, so producers keep a larger share of the final price.

questions.stem_md: A member of an imagined village dairy cooperative pours 10 litres of milk a day at ₹40 a litre. How much (in ₹) is she paid for 30 days?
questions.solution_md:
Step 1: Payment = litres a day × price × days.
Step 2: 10 × 40 × 30 = ₹12,000.

questions.stem_md: Explain three ways in which dairy cooperatives have helped rural households.
questions.solution_md: Income, removal of intermediaries, and services or empowerment.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Fair, regular income**: members are paid by quantity and quality, often weekly, which steadies household income.
2. **No middlemen**: the cooperative processes and sells milk, so the producer keeps more of the price.
3. **Support and empowerment**: veterinary care, feed and training are provided, and **women**, who do much of the dairy work, gain income of their own.

questions.stem_md: Agricultural diversification has two aspects:

options.text_md: more fertiliser use and more pesticide use
selling crops abroad and importing food
a change in the cropping pattern, and a shift of workers from crop farming to allied and non-farm activities
buying more land and hiring more labourers

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** a change in the cropping pattern, and a shift of workers from crop farming to allied and non-farm activities. Diversification means growing a wider range of crops, and moving part of the workforce into livestock, fisheries, horticulture and non-farm work. The other pairs are not what the term means.

questions.stem_md: Why is diversification especially important for rain-fed farming regions?

options.text_md: Rain-fed regions have too much irrigation already
Diversification stops all rainfall variation
Depending on one crop and the rains is risky, and other activities give work and income when the crop fails or in the off-season
It removes the need for any credit

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Depending on one crop and the rains is risky, and other activities give work and income when the crop fails or in the off-season. Farm income in rain-fed areas is uncertain and seasonal; other activities spread the risk and provide work through the year. Diversification does not change rainfall or end the need for credit.

questions.stem_md: A farming family in an imagined village of Rajasthan keeps goats and a few cows along with its millet crop. The main advantage is that

options.text_md: livestock gives income and food even when the crop fails, so the family's risk is lower
animals guarantee the millet crop a higher yield every year
the family no longer needs any water
the government buys all their goats at the MSP

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** livestock gives income and food even when the crop fails, so the family's risk is lower. Mixed farming spreads risk: milk and the sale of animals continue in a drought year. Livestock does not guarantee yields, remove water needs or come under MSP.

questions.stem_md: Horticulture includes the growing of

options.text_md: only wheat and rice
only cotton and jute
only timber trees in forests
fruits, vegetables, flowers, medicinal and aromatic plants, and spices

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** fruits, vegetables, flowers, medicinal and aromatic plants, and spices. Horticulture covers fruits, vegetables, flowers, spices, plantation crops, and medicinal and aromatic plants. Cereals, fibres and forest timber are other activities.

questions.stem_md: In an imagined coastal village of Odisha, the men go out to sea while many women dry, process and sell the fish. This shows that fisheries

options.text_md: are part of the secondary sector only
create non-crop work for whole families, including women
need no credit or marketing
are possible only in rivers

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** create non-crop work for whole families, including women. Fishing, processing and selling provide work for both men and women outside crop farming. Fisheries need credit and marketing, and include marine as well as inland waters.

questions.stem_md: Which is the best example of information technology helping rural development?

options.text_md: A mobile service that tells farmers the weather forecast and crop prices in nearby markets
A farmer ploughing his field with bullocks
A moneylender writing loans in a paper register
A trader using a faulty weighing scale

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** A mobile service that tells farmers the weather forecast and crop prices in nearby markets. Timely weather and price information helps farmers plan and sell better, and such services also create rural jobs. The other examples involve no IT.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Non-farm activities are an important source of rural employment.

**Reason (R):** Crop farming in many areas provides work for only part of the year, leaving workers idle in the off-season.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Both are true, and R explains A: because farming is seasonal, non-farm work such as processing, crafts and services fills the gap.

questions.stem_md: True or false? Agricultural diversification means growing only cereals over a wider area.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: **False.** Diversification means moving to a wider range of crops and activities, such as fruits, vegetables, livestock and fisheries, not concentrating on cereals.

questions.stem_md: Match each imagined rural enterprise with the activity it represents.

options.text_md: A poultry unit of 500 birds in Namakkal district
A pond raising rohu and catla in West Bengal
A marigold and rose farm near Bengaluru
A village unit making pickles and papad

questions.solution_md: **Key:** (a)–(s), (b)–(q), (c)–(r), (d)–(p). Poultry is animal husbandry; pond fish are inland fisheries; flowers are floriculture within horticulture; pickles and papad are food processing, a non-farm activity.

questions.stem_md: An imagined farm household earns ₹60,000 a year from crops, ₹30,000 from dairy and ₹10,000 from poultry. What percentage of its income comes from activities other than crops?
What are the two aspects of agricultural diversification?
questions.solution_md: Name and explain both aspects.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Change in cropping pattern**: moving from mainly food grains to a wider range of crops such as fruits, vegetables, oilseeds and flowers.
2. **Shift of workers** from crop farming to **allied activities** (livestock, fisheries, poultry) and **non-farm work** (processing, crafts, services).

marking_scheme.step: Shift of workforce to allied and non-farm work

questions.stem_md: Explain two ways in which animal husbandry helps small and landless rural families.
questions.solution_md: Income stability and suitability for families with little or no land.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. It gives a **steady income** from milk, eggs or meat through the year, even when crops fail.
2. It needs **little land**, so landless and women-headed families can keep a few animals, and dung gives **manure and fuel**.

questions.stem_md: How can horticulture raise incomes and employment in rural areas? Give three points.
questions.solution_md: Three linked benefits: value per acre, labour use, and processing or trade.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Higher value**: fruits, vegetables and flowers often earn more per acre than cereals.
2. **More work**: picking, grading, packing and transport employ many people, including **women**.
3. **Links to processing and export**: juice, pickle and spice units and exports create further jobs and income.

questions.stem_md: Why is diversification into productive non-farm activities necessary for rural India? Explain with reference to any three such activities.
questions.solution_md: Why diversification is needed, then three activities with how each helps.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Need**: crop farming is **seasonal and risky**, especially where it depends on rain; it cannot employ the growing rural workforce all year.
2. **Spreading risk**: other sources of income protect families when a crop fails.
3. **Animal husbandry**: cattle, goats and poultry give **regular income** and suit families with little land.
4. **Fisheries**: inland and marine fishing, processing and selling provide work for men and **women**.
5. **Horticulture and agro-processing**: fruits, flowers and processing units earn more per acre and create jobs; **IT** services add information and new work. Diversification therefore gives **productive employment** and steadier incomes.

marking_scheme.step: Seasonality and risk of crop farming

questions.stem_md: Evaluate the role of information technology in rural development.
questions.solution_md: Four uses with benefits and one set of limitations, with a judgement.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Information for farming**: weather forecasts, crop advice and soil information help farmers plan better.
2. **Prices and markets**: knowing prices in nearby markets lets farmers choose where and when to sell.
3. **Services**: online access to government schemes, land records and banking saves time and reduces middlemen.
4. **Jobs**: village service centres and data work create employment for educated rural youth.
5. **Limits**: weak connectivity, low digital literacy and cost keep many poor households out. IT is a powerful tool when supported by **skills and connectivity**.

questions.stem_md: Organic farming is a system of cultivation that

options.text_md: uses the largest possible amount of chemical fertilisers
relies on organic manure, compost and natural pest control instead of chemical fertilisers and pesticides
grows crops only inside factories
depends only on imported hybrid seeds

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** relies on organic manure, compost and natural pest control instead of chemical fertilisers and pesticides. Organic farming restores and maintains ecological balance by using natural inputs and avoiding synthetic chemicals. The other options describe intensive chemical farming or unrelated practices.

questions.stem_md: Which is a benefit of organic farming for **small farmers**?

options.text_md: Yields always double in the first year
Organic produce never spoils
Inputs such as compost can be made on the farm, so costs are lower
No labour is needed

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Inputs such as compost can be made on the farm, so costs are lower. On-farm inputs replace costly purchased chemicals. Yields often fall at first, organic produce can have a shorter shelf life, and organic methods usually need more labour.

questions.stem_md: Which is a genuine **limitation** of organic farming?

options.text_md: It always harms soil fertility
It uses more chemical pesticides than modern farming
There is no demand for organic food anywhere
Yields may fall in the early years, and organic produce may have a shorter shelf life

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Yields may fall in the early years, and organic produce may have a shorter shelf life. Lower early yields and perishability are real problems. Organic farming improves soil health, avoids chemical pesticides and has growing demand.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Organic farming can create more employment in rural areas.

**Reason (R):** Organic methods such as composting and manual weeding need more labour than chemical farming.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Both are true, and R explains A: more labour-intensive methods mean more work per acre.

questions.stem_md: True or false? A farmer who switches to organic farming can expect higher yields than before from the very first season.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: **False.** Yields often dip in the first few years while the soil recovers and natural pest control builds up.

questions.stem_md: On one acre of an imagined farm, chemical farming gives 40 quintals sold at ₹2,000 a quintal, with input costs of ₹12,000. Organic farming gives 34 quintals sold at ₹2,500 a quintal, with input costs of ₹5,000. By how much (in ₹) is the organic net income higher?
State two benefits of organic farming.
questions.solution_md: Any two: sustainability, health, lower input costs, export demand, more employment.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. It **protects the environment**: soil, water and helpful insects are not damaged by chemicals, so farming is **sustainable**.
2. It gives **healthier food** and can earn **higher prices** in domestic and export markets.

questions.stem_md: Explain three problems that limit the spread of organic farming in India.
questions.solution_md: Three distinct barriers: yield, market access or certification, and perishability.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Lower early yields**: output may fall for a few years, which small farmers cannot afford.
2. **Marketing and certification**: farmers need awareness, certification and buyers willing to pay a premium.
3. **Short shelf life** and limited choice of off-season produce, with too little storage and transport for perishable organic food.

questions.stem_md: Organic farming is often called the answer to the problems of chemical farming. Evaluate this view.
questions.solution_md: Meaning, benefits on three fronts, limitations, then a balanced judgement.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Meaning**: farming with **compost, manure and natural pest control**, avoiding synthetic chemicals.
2. **Environment**: it restores **soil health** and avoids polluting water, so it is **sustainable**.
3. **Economics**: on-farm inputs cut costs, and **premium prices** and export demand can raise income; it is **labour-intensive**, creating rural work.
4. **Health**: food free of chemical residues.
5. **Limits**: **lower early yields**, **shorter shelf life**, the need for certification and marketing, and the question of feeding a large population. So it is a valuable path, especially for some crops and regions, but it needs **support in transition** and markets rather than being a complete answer by itself.

questions.stem_md: Study the table and answer the questions that follow. *(Imagined village and figures, written by SOYL for practice.)*
questions.solution_md:
**(a)** Step 1: Banks + cooperative = 45 + 22 = 67 lakh.
Step 2: Share = 67 ÷ 100 × 100 = 67 per cent.

**(b)** Read the survey note under the table.

**(c) (i)** Two reasons rooted in access barriers and convenience.

**OR (c) (ii)** Two workable steps that widen access to institutional credit.
